## Introduction

### Course Overview

R is a powerful programming language and environment for statistical computing and data visualization. In this course, you will learn:

- How to interact with R using Positron or RStudio
- Creating and manipulating R objects
- Working with different data types and structures
- Loading and working with real datasets

This lecture provides a foundational introduction to R programming that you'll use throughout the course.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this page, you should be able to:

- Use Positron or RStudio effectively
- Create and manipulate R objects
- Understand R data types and structures
- Write and run R code in scripts
- Load and explore datasets
:::

## R Programming Fundamentals

### What is R?

**R is:**

- A programming language for **statistical computing** and **data visualization**
- **Open-source and free** software
- A **dynamic programming language** that automatically interprets your code as you run it
- Platform independent (Windows, Mac, Linux)

An **integrated development environment (IDE)** makes R much easier to use. This course supports two free IDEs from Posit: **Positron** (the newer one, built for data science in R and Python) and **RStudio** (the long-standing R IDE). Everything in these notes works in either; where the steps differ, both are shown.

### Why Learn R?

R has become the standard tool for data analysis and statistical computing in:

- Academic research
- Data science and analytics
- Biostatistics and epidemiology
- Business intelligence

Key advantages include:

- Extensive package ecosystem (more than 20,000 packages)
- Publication-quality graphics
- Reproducible research capabilities
- Strong community support

### Your IDE: Positron or RStudio

Both IDEs show the same four kinds of information, arranged a little differently.

| What it does | Positron | RStudio |
|---|---|---|
| Write and save code (`.R`, `.qmd`) | **Editor** (center) | **Source** pane (top left) |
| Run code and see results | **Console** (bottom) | **Console** (bottom left) |
| See the objects you created | **Variables** in the Session pane (right) | **Environment** tab (top right) |
| Files, plots, help, packages | **Explorer** (left), **Plots** (Session pane), **Help**, **Viewer**, and **Packages** panes | **Files / Plots / Packages / Help** (bottom right) |

**Work in a project folder.** Keep everything for one analysis (code, data, output) in one folder. In Positron, use **File → Open Folder**; in RStudio, use **File → New Project**. R then reads and writes files relative to that folder, so you never need `setwd()` and your code runs on any computer.

#### Customizing your workspace

- **Positron:** open **Settings** (Ctrl/Cmd + ,) to change the color theme, fonts, and editor options.
- **RStudio:** **Tools → Global Options** changes the theme, fonts, and pane layout.
- A dark theme can reduce eye strain during long coding sessions.

## Working with the Console

### Basic R Commands

The console is where you type commands and see results. Let's start with simple arithmetic:

```{r}
#| label: basic-arithmetic
# Simple addition
1 + 1

# Division
10 / 2

# Exponentiation
2 ^ 3

# Square root
sqrt(16)
```

### Understanding R Output

Notice the `[1]` prefix in the output. This indicates the **position of the first value** displayed on that line.

```{r}
#| label: output-index
# When displaying many values, you see multiple indices
100:130
```

Each line of output starts with the position of its first value in square brackets: `[1]` on the first line, and on the next line the position where that line picks up (how many values fit on a line depends on the width of your console).

::: {.callout-tip}
**Tip:** The `[1]` notation becomes especially useful when working with vectors and matrices where you need to track the position of values.
:::

### Incomplete Commands

If you type an incomplete command and press Enter, R displays a `+` prompt, waiting for you to complete it:

```{r}
#| label: incomplete-command-demo
#| eval: false
# Type this but don't press Enter after the minus sign
5 -
# Then press Enter and the prompt will show +
# Type 1 and press Enter
1
```

When you do this in R, you'll see:

```{r}
#| label: incomplete-example
#| eval: false
> 5 -
+ 1
[1] 4
```

To cancel an incomplete command, press **Escape** and start over.

### Error Messages

If you type a command that R doesn't recognize, you'll get an error message:

```{r}
#| label: error-example
#| eval: false
> 3 % 5
Error: unexpected input in "3 % 5"
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Error messages are helpful! They tell you what went wrong. Don't be intimidated by them: they're just R's way of saying it didn't understand your command. The `%` operator is used for different purposes in R, and `3 % 5` is not valid syntax.
:::

### Canceling Long-Running Commands

Some R commands take a long time to run. To cancel a running command:

- **Positron:** click the interrupt (stop) button in the Console action bar.
- **RStudio:** press **Esc** with the cursor in the Console, or click the red **STOP** sign at the top of the Console.

Canceling may take a moment.

## R Objects and Assignment

### Creating Objects

R lets you save data by storing it in **objects**. An object is simply a name you can use to retrieve stored data.

You assign values to objects using `<-` or `=`:

```{r}
#| label: object-creation
# Create an object named 'a' with value 1
a <- 1

# View the contents
a

# Do arithmetic with the object
a + 2

# Create another object
b <- 10
a + b
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**Best Practice:** Use `<-` for assignment in R. While `=` also works, `<-` is the R convention and makes your code more readable to other R users.
:::

#### Reassigning Objects

R will overwrite an object without asking for confirmation:

```{r}
#| label: object-reassignment
# First assignment
a <- 1
a

# Reassign a new value
a <- 2
a

# You can overwrite with different data types
a <- "text"
a
```

### Naming Conventions

Object names in R have a few rules:

**Valid names start with:**

- A letter or period (`.variable_name`)
- Can contain numbers, letters, underscores, and periods

**Invalid names:**

- Start with a number: `2variables` (not allowed)
- Contain special symbols: `my-var`, `my$var`, `my@var` (not allowed)

```{r}
#| label: naming-examples
#| eval: false
# Valid names
my_variable <- 5
my.variable <- 5
myVariable <- 5
x1 <- 10

# Invalid names (these will produce errors)
1variable <- 5        # Error: starts with number
my-variable <- 5      # Error: hyphen not allowed
my variable <- 5      # Error: space not allowed
```

#### Case Sensitivity

R **is case-sensitive**, so `name` and `Name` are different objects:

```{r}
#| label: case-sensitivity
name <- "lowercase"
Name <- "uppercase"

name
Name
```

### Listing Objects in Your Environment

Use `ls()` to see all objects you've created:

```{r}
#| label: listing-objects
# Create some objects
x <- 5
y <- 10
z <- "hello"

# List all objects
ls()

# Remove a specific object
rm(z)

# Verify it's gone
ls()
```

## R Data Types and Structures

### Data Types

R has several basic data types:

#### Numeric

```{r}
#| label: numeric-data
# Numeric (default for numbers)
x <- 3.14
y <- 42

class(x)
class(y)
```

#### Character

```{r}
#| label: character-data
# Character (text)
name <- "Alice"
greeting <- 'Hello, world!'

class(name)
class(greeting)
```

#### Logical

```{r}
#| label: logical-data
# Logical (TRUE/FALSE)
is_patient <- TRUE
treatment_received <- FALSE

class(is_patient)
```

### Vectors

A **vector** is a collection of values of the same type. Create vectors using `c()`:

```{r}
#| label: vectors
# Numeric vector
ages <- c(25, 30, 35, 40, 45)

# Character vector
names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave", "Eve")

# Logical vector
is_smoker <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

# Check length
length(ages)

# Access individual elements
names[2]      # Second element
ages[c(1, 3)] # First and third elements
```

### Sequences and Repetition

```{r}
#| label: sequences
# Create sequences
1:10           # Sequence from 1 to 10
seq(1, 10, by = 2)  # Sequence with step

# Repeat values
rep(1, 5)      # Repeat 1 five times
rep(c("A", "B"), 3)  # Repeat vector three times
```

### Lists

A **list** is a collection where elements can have different types:

```{r}
#| label: lists
# Create a list
person <- list(
  name = "Alice",
  age = 30,
  is_student = FALSE
)

# Access elements
person$name
person[[2]]  # Access by position
person[["age"]]  # Access by name

# View the list structure
str(person)
```

### Matrices

A **matrix** is a two-dimensional collection of elements all of the same type:

```{r}
#| label: matrices
# Create a 3x3 matrix
m <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9), nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m

# Access elements
m[1, 2]      # Row 1, Column 2
m[2, ]       # All of Row 2
m[, 3]       # All of Column 3

# Matrix operations
t(m)         # Transpose
m %*% m      # Matrix multiplication
```

### Data Frames

**Data frames** are the most important data structure in R for statistical analysis. They're like spreadsheets where:

- Each column is a **variable**
- Each row is an **observation**
- Columns can have different data types

```{r}
#| label: dataframes
# Create a simple data frame
df <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave", "Eve"),
  Age = c(28, 35, 42, 31, 29),
  Diagnosis = c("Yes", "No", "Yes", "No", "No")
)

df

# Check structure
str(df)

# Dimensions
dim(df)
nrow(df)
ncol(df)
```

### Accessing Data Frame Elements

```{r}
#| label: dataframe-access
# Access a column using $
df$Name

# Access by row and column
df[1, 2]      # Row 1, Column 2

# Access entire column
df[, "Age"]
df[, 3]

# Access entire row
df[2, ]

# Subset rows where Age > 30
df[df$Age > 30, ]
```

## Reading Data

### Loading CSV Files

In epidemiological research, you'll usually start with existing data:

```{r}
#| label: reading-csv
#| eval: false
# Read a CSV file
data <- read.csv("path/to/file.csv")

# If first row contains variable names (default)
data <- read.csv("data.csv")

# If no header row
data <- read.csv("data.csv", header = FALSE)

# Specify missing value codes
data <- read.csv("data.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA", "."))
```

#### Using an import dialog

**Easier method for point-and-click:**

Both IDEs have a dialog that writes the import code for you. In **Positron**, use **File → Import Data** (also on the Variables pane toolbar, or right-click a data file in the Explorer). In **RStudio**:

1. Click **Environment** tab → **Import Dataset** → **From Text (readr)...**
2. Browse to your file
3. Preview the data and adjust settings
4. Click **Import** - RStudio generates the code

**Copy this code to your script** for reproducibility:

```{r}
#| label: import-example
#| eval: false
# Code generated by RStudio
library(readr)
mydata <- read_csv("myfile.csv")
```

::: {.highlight}
Always save the import code in your script. This creates a reproducible record of how you loaded your data.
:::

## R Scripts

### What is an R Script?

An **R script** is a plain text file containing R code. Scripts allow you to:

- Write and save your code
- Create a reproducible record of your analysis
- Rerun your entire analysis anytime
- Share your code with others

#### Creating a New Script

**Positron:** **File → New File...** and choose **R File** (or Quarto Document for a `.qmd`).

**RStudio:** **File → New File → R Script**, or **Ctrl + Shift + N** (Windows/Linux) / **Cmd + Shift + N** (Mac).

### Best Practices for Scripts

#### 1. Add Comments

Use `#` to add comments that explain your code:

```{r}
#| label: script-example
# Create sample patient data
set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(
  age = rnorm(100, mean = 55, sd = 15),
  weight = rnorm(100, mean = 80, sd = 12),
  height = rnorm(100, mean = 1.70, sd = 0.10)
)

# Calculate BMI
data$BMI <- data$weight / (data$height^2)

# Subset to patients over 50 years old
older_patients <- data[data$age > 50, ]

# Summarize BMI for older patients
summary(older_patients$BMI)
```

#### 2. Organize Your Script

Start with header information and load all packages:

```{r}
#| label: organized-script
#| eval: false
# =====================================================
# Analysis of NHANES Data
# Author: Muntasir Masum
# Date: January 22, 2026
# =====================================================

# Load required packages
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(NHANES)

# -----
# 1. Load and Prepare Data
# -----
data(NHANES)
head(NHANES)

# -----
# 2. Exploratory Data Analysis
# -----
summary(NHANES)
NHANES |>
  group_by(Gender) |>
  summarise(mean_age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_bp_sys = mean(BPSys1, na.rm = TRUE))

# -----
# 3. Statistical Tests
# -----
t.test(BPSys1 ~ Gender, data = NHANES)
```

#### 3. Use Meaningful Names

```{r}
#| label: naming-conventions
# Good names
systolic_bp <- 140
patient_age <- 55
calculate_bmi <- function(weight, height) { weight / height^2 }

# Poor names
sb <- 140          # Unclear abbreviation
a <- 55            # Single letter
f1 <- function(w, h) { w / h^2 }  # Cryptic
```

### Running Code from a Script

**Run a single line:**

- Click the line and press **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows/Linux) / **Cmd + Return** (Mac)
- In RStudio you can also click the **Run** button

**Run multiple lines:**

- Highlight them and press **Ctrl + Enter** / **Cmd + Return**

**Run the entire script:**

- **Positron:** click the **Run** (play) button at the top right of the editor, or **Ctrl + Shift + Enter** / **Cmd + Shift + Return**
- **RStudio:** click the **Source** button, or **Ctrl + Shift + S** / **Cmd + Shift + S**

## Practical Example

### Complete Workflow

Let's work through a complete analysis workflow using the NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) dataset:

```{r}
#| label: complete-workflow
#| message: false
# Load required packages
library(NHANES)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Load the data
data(NHANES)

# 2. Examine the data
head(NHANES)
str(NHANES)
```

```{r}
#| label: workflow-continued
#| message: false
# 3. Calculate summary statistics by gender
summary_stats <- NHANES |>
  group_by(Gender) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_age = sd(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bp_sys = mean(BPSys1, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_bp_sys = sd(BPSys1, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_bmi = sd(BMI, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

print(summary_stats)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-gender
#| fig-cap: "Systolic blood pressure by gender in the NHANES package data"
#| fig-alt: "Box plots with jittered points of first-reading systolic blood pressure for female and male NHANES participants. Both groups center near 115 to 120 mmHg with long upper tails past 200 mmHg; the male median is slightly higher."
#| message: false
# 4. Visualize the data
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(NHANES, aes(x = Gender, y = BPSys1, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "Systolic Blood Pressure by Gender",
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)",
       x = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r}
#| label: workflow-stats
#| message: false
# 5. Conduct statistical test
# Remove rows with missing blood pressure data
nhanes_clean <- NHANES |>
  filter(!is.na(BPSys1))

# Compare systolic blood pressure between genders
t_test <- t.test(BPSys1 ~ Gender, data = nhanes_clean)
print(t_test)
```

**Free Online Resources:**

- [Hands-on Programming with R](https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/) - Great for beginners

```{r}
#| label: swirl
#| eval: false
install.packages("swirl")
library(swirl)
swirl()
```

### Useful Packages for Epidemiology

- **dplyr** - Data manipulation
- **ggplot2** - Data visualization
- **tidyr** - Data reshaping
- **epiDisplay** - Epidemiological tables
- **epitools** - Epidemiological calculations
- **survival** - Survival analysis

## Key Concepts Summary

::: {.callout-tip}

### Essential Points to Remember

1. **R Objects:** Use `<-` to assign values to named objects

2. **Vectors:** Combine multiple values with `c()`

3. **Functions:** Call functions with syntax `function_name(argument1, argument2)`

4. **Data Frames:** The primary structure for statistical analysis in R

5. **Scripts:** Always write and save your code in scripts for reproducibility

6. **Help:** Use `?function_name` or `help(function_name)` for documentation

7. **Comments:** Use `#` to explain your code for future reference

8. **Project folders:** Keep each analysis in its own folder and open that folder (Positron) or project (RStudio); `getwd()` shows where R looks for files, and you should not need `setwd()`

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
